headline: Markets open the week still shaking off Friday's AI-led selloff
body: Wall Street starts the new week digesting Friday's drop, its worst single session since June: the Nasdaq 100 fell roughly 3.5% and the S&P 500 about 1.8%, breaking below its 100-day moving average as weak guidance from Amazon and a brutal decline in Intel overshadowed an otherwise solid earnings season. That capped a rough October for growth stocks specifically — the Nasdaq posted its worst month since March 2025 while the S&P 500 also finished the month lower, a reversal from the record highs set earlier in the year. Money moved toward safety alongside the equity selling: Treasuries caught a bid and yields eased, consistent with investors trimming exposure to the AI-infrastructure spenders that had carried most of the market's gains this year rather than a broader loss of risk appetite.

Breadth told a more nuanced story than the headline indices suggest — small-caps and defensive sectors actually held up or gained over the same week even as the mega-cap AI leaders were sold hard, pointing to rotation rather than wholesale capitulation. That lines up with at least one widely watched sentiment gauge, which slid from a neutral reading two weeks earlier into 'extreme fear' territory by late October as the string of disappointing AI-capex commentary piled up. Retail and social-media chatter offered little concrete signal today, so this read leans more on price action and earnings-driven headlines than on any specific forum or meme-stock narrative — the dominant story remains a reassessment of how much more AI spending the market is willing to reward, not a broad flight from stocks.
